title: The safe bet
hook: live as though actions have results; you lose nothing either way

segments.voice: Yesterday: vedana, feeling, counted many ways. Your line: many ways to count.

A village called Sālā, in the kingdom of Kosala. Its people have heard a lot of traveling teachers. One says there is another world after this one. Another says there isn't, and that nothing you do carries forward. Each one is very sure. Then the Buddha arrives, and before he teaches anything, he asks a question. Is there a teacher here you trust? And the villagers say, honestly: no. They've heard too many confident voices. What would you say to a village like that?
screen: `A VILLAGE CALLED SĀLĀ.` → `TOO MANY CONFIDENT VOICES.` → `IS THERE A TEACHER YOU TRUST? NO.`

segments.voice: The answer is in the sixtieth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings. He doesn't try to out-argue the other teachers. He offers what the sutta calls apaṇṇaka, a teaching that's sure, that can't go wrong. Take two people. The first holds that there is no other world, that giving bears no fruit, that good and bad actions have no results. So he lives carelessly in body, speech and mind. The second holds that actions do have results, and lives carefully. Now, says the Buddha, suppose the first is right, and there is no other world. Even then, the wise call the careless one a person of bad conduct, here and now. And if there is another world, he loses twice. The careful one? If there's no other world, the wise still praise her here and now. If there is, she gains there too. The sutta borrows a word from dice: she has made the winning throw, and it wins both ways. Notice what he doesn't ask for. He doesn't say: believe in rebirth first, and then be good. The question can stay open, and the way to live comes out the same. Buddhist traditions teach rebirth, and this sutta also speaks to the listener who isn't sure yet. It asks one thing: live as if what you do has results. On an ordinary Tuesday, that might mean telling the truth on a form nobody checks. You don't have to settle the universe first. The bet pays in this life, and again if there's another.
screen: `APAṆṆAKA: A TEACHING THAT CAN'T GO WRONG.` · `TWO PEOPLE, TWO VIEWS.` · `IF THERE'S NO NEXT WORLD, STILL PRAISED.` · `THE WINNING THROW, BOTH WAYS.` · then, large: `THE SAFE BET.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one choice waiting for you later, a message, a purchase, a conversation, and ask it two questions slowly: if nothing I do echoes past today, is this worth doing well? And if it does echo, further than I can see? Let the answers arrive on the out-breath, notice whether they point the same way, and rest there.
Apannaka. Sure, beyond dispute: live as though actions have results, and you come out ahead whether or not there is another world.
Your line: wins either way. A careful life is praised here, and gains there too. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Buddhist teachers use this sutta when talking with people who doubt rebirth: the advice to keep the precepts and act carefully stands either way, so it can be practiced before the big questions are settled.

original.note: Pali apaṇṇaka: sure, beyond dispute. it is the title of this sutta, and of the first tale in the Jataka collection.

what a scholar hears: apaṇṇaka, 'incontrovertible', with the dice words kaṭaggaha and kaliggaha for the winning and losing throw; the Jataka collection opens with a tale of the same name.

chat.says: I'm not sure about rebirth. Does Buddhism still have anything for me?
options: The Buddha's safe bet: live as if actions have results, and you win either way.
No; you have to settle the question of rebirth before doing any good.
Only if you agree that actions have no results beyond this life.
chat.meaning: In MN 60 the careful life wins both ways: praised by the wise here and now, and gaining again if there is another world.

Sālā.meaning: a village in the kingdom of Kosala

Kosala.meaning: a kingdom of the Buddha's time

apaṇṇaka.meaning: sure, beyond dispute: a teaching that can't go wrong

Middle-Length Sayings.meaning: the Majjhima Nikaya, a collection of the Buddha's talks

notes: MN 60 paraphrased throughout; please check the order of the wager (bad conduct censured 'here and now' by the wise; the winning throw kaṭaggaha / losing throw kaliggaha) against the Pali.
The careful person is given 'she' and the careless 'he' for variety; the sutta speaks of a person (purisapuggala). Change if preferred.
'Buddhists differ on how literally to take rebirth' is a deliberately light line; a Keeper may want different wording.
Some readers compare this sutta to Pascal's wager; left out of the script to avoid comparing traditions.
